newsitem.title: USA: CFTC orders CBOT to fix grain problem.
newsitem.headline: CFTC orders CBOT to fix grain problem.

text.p: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission, in an unprecedented move, Thursday ordered the Chicago Board of Trade to submit a plan within 75 days to deal with a shortage of grain storage capacity.
The futures markets regulator said the CBOT, the world's largest futures market, should increase the capacity and number of locations needed to meet corn and soybean futures contracts.
The CFTC commissioners voted 5-0 to give the CBOT until March 4 to fix the problem. Otherwise, the agency said, it will impose its own solution.

In issuing the order, the agency invoked an obscure provision of the Commodity Exchange Act for the first time. The provision empowers the agency to give an exchange 75 days to make appropriate changes in its delivery rules if those rules fail to meet legal requirements.
As part of its action, the CFTC also ordered the CBOT to review its wheat delivery system in the next 120 days.
The CFTC, at an open meeting, said that with the "precipitous drop" in grain storage capacity in Chicago within the past 14 months, the problem has reached a critical juncture.
According to CFTC Commissioner Joseph Dial, CBOT's storage capacity has been slashed to 14.7 million bushels for grain, a drop of 75 percent since 1995.

Against this background, trading volume for corn has grown eightfold and soybeans fourfold since the 1970s, sparked by an 80 percent rise in combined annual U.S. production for those crops over the past 25 years, the agency said.
The inadequate storage space may make CBOT contracts vulnerable to market manipulation or "squeeze," thus affecting prices on the exchange, the CFTC feared.
"Based on the evidence presented to the commission, the potential for manipulation of the corn and soybean contracts in the current environment is real," said CFTC Commissioner Barbara Holum.
CFTC Chairwoman Brooksley Born urged the CBOT to act promptly in resolving the issue. She said she preferred that the CBOT formulate its own solution and "do so promptly."
"Otherwise, the CFTC will be forced to act," she said.
"We are giving the exchange one more opportunity to align its delivery terms with the realities of the cash market," added CFTC Commissioner Joseph Dial.

In its order, the CFTC included four possible alternatives that the CBOT may adopt. It said it was not forcing the CBOT to adopt any of the alternatives, but noted they are examples of how the exchange might meet requirements of the commodities law.
In any case,the CFTC specified that any contract changes the CBOT proposes should provide linkage with the cash market.
If the CFTC acts, it said its move would not apply to outstanding futures contracts.

In October, CBOT members rejected a plan drafted by a market task force to raise the number of locations available for grain delivery. The plan would have allowed corn, wheat and soybeans to be delivered against futures contracts in Chicago, Toledo, Milwaukee and the Illinois River, and would have eliminated St. Louis.
Reacting to Thursday's CFTC order, the CBOT announced it was forming a new corn and soybean delivery task force.

"We were fully aware of the need to increase grain storage capacity in Chicago," said market spokeswoman Deborah Kostroun. "Chairman Patrick Arbor was already planning to form a new delivery task force in January."
